evidence.claim: Article 89, fraction X, gives the president authority to direct foreign policy and conclude treaties, subject to Senate approval, and requires peaceful settlement and non-use-of-force principles.
evidence.title: Constitución Política de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos
evidence.excerpt: Article 89, fraction X, gives the president authority to direct foreign policy and conclude treaties, subject to Senate approval, and requires peaceful settlement and non-use-of-force principles.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official constitutional text; directly states the executive's foreign-policy power and constraints.
evidence.ruler_attribution: AMLO had treaty-diplomacy authority in 2022, but the legal text is institutional rather than personal nuclear-risk evidence.
contrary_evidence: The Senate remains a real constraint.
These powers concern diplomacy, not weapons custody or nuclear command.

evidence.claim: Mexico has safeguards agreements in force covering the Treaty of Tlatelolco, the NPT, and an additional protocol to the safeguards arrangement.
evidence.title: Country List : Office of Legal Affairs : IAEA
evidence.excerpt: Mexico has safeguards agreements in force covering the Treaty of Tlatelolco, the NPT, and an additional protocol to the safeguards arrangement.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Authoritative IAEA legal registry for country safeguards status.
evidence.period_fit: Strong inherited-baseline fit for 2022; the registry is current but the agreements were already in force.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State-level safeguard architecture inherited by AMLO; not a personal nuclear-command act.
contrary_evidence: This shows peaceful-use monitoring, not proof of perfect safety.
It is institutional context, not evidence of a 2022 AMLO decision.

evidence.claim: Mexico’s operating nuclear fleet consists of two civilian reactors at Laguna Verde, both in operational status.
evidence.title: PRIS - Country Details
evidence.excerpt: Mexico’s operating nuclear fleet consists of two civilian reactors at Laguna Verde, both in operational status.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: IAEA PRIS is the standard authoritative reactor-status database.
evidence.period_fit: Moderate fit: current registry, but the civilian reactor configuration is stable and consistent with the 2022 period.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Civilian nuclear infrastructure under Mexican state oversight; not evidence of weapons authority or nuclear escalation.
contrary_evidence: A civilian nuclear sector still creates safety and regulatory responsibility.
The page does not show AMLO personally changing reactor safety policy in 2022.

evidence.claim: The CTBTO status table records Mexico as having signed the CTBT on 24 September 1996 and ratified it on 5 October 1999.
evidence.title: Status of Signature and Ratification
evidence.excerpt: The CTBTO status table records Mexico as having signed the CTBT on 24 September 1996 and ratified it on 5 October 1999.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: CTBTO treaty-status table is authoritative for signature and ratification dates.
evidence.ruler_attribution: This is inherited disarmament posture, not AMLO-specific conduct.
contrary_evidence: The CTBT is about testing restraint, not a full measure of existential-risk governance.
No 2022 AMLO-specific testing decision appears here.

evidence.claim: Mexico welcomed the first meeting of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons states parties and said it was one of the treaty's architects, reaffirming its leadership in nuclear disarmament.
evidence.title: Conclusion of the first meeting of the Nuclear Weapons Ban Treaty in Vienna
evidence.excerpt: Mexico welcomed the first meeting of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons states parties and said it was one of the treaty's architects, reaffirming its leadership in nuclear disarmament.
evidence.source_locator: Headline, opening paragraph, and first bullet points
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary foreign-ministry statement, contemporaneous and directly relevant to 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Government of Mexico under AMLO, but this is institutional foreign-policy signaling rather than a unique personal nuclear-risk choice.
contrary_evidence: The source is celebratory and self-presenting.
It shows stance and diplomacy, not technical command or safety reform.

evidence.claim: The Foreign Ministry hosted the eighth annual Summer School on Nuclear Disarmament and Nonproliferation for diplomats from Latin America and the Caribbean, with 23 officials from 22 countries participating.
evidence.title: Conclusion of the 8th Summer School on Nuclear Disarmament and Nonproliferation at the Foreign Ministry
evidence.excerpt: The Foreign Ministry hosted the eighth annual Summer School on Nuclear Disarmament and Nonproliferation for diplomats from Latin America and the Caribbean, with 23 officials from 22 countries participating.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary institutional release with a clear date and program description.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional capacity-building under AMLO’s administration; not a direct personal nuclear-command act.
contrary_evidence: Training and convening are supportive but indirect.
This does not prove any specific 2022 risk-bearing decision by AMLO himself.

evidence.claim: The article’s abstract says disarmament has been on Mexico’s foreign-policy agenda for 60 years and asks whether nuclear disarmament is practicable in light of 21st-century security realities.
evidence.title: La deslegitimación de las armas, el desarme y la protección de la seguridad humana
evidence.excerpt: The article’s abstract says disarmament has been on Mexico’s foreign-policy agenda for 60 years and asks whether nuclear disarmament is practicable in light of 21st-century security realities.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Published analytical piece from a Mexican foreign-policy journal; useful context, but it is interpretive rather than a primary record.
evidence.period_fit: Exact 2022 publication date, though the analysis is general rather than AMLO-specific.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Contextual to Mexico’s policy tradition; not direct evidence of AMLO’s own decision-making.
contrary_evidence: Interpretive scholarship can overgeneralize from tradition.
It does not identify a specific 2022 nuclear-risk choice by AMLO.

unresolved_gaps: Federal command attribution is still thin for several state-level protest, journalist, and policing incidents.
Independent evidence that AMLO strengthened courts, the INE, INAI, or other checks is still weak compared with the evidence of media hostility and electoral-pressure attempts.
Direct personal-nexus evidence on self-enrichment, hidden ownership, or preferential benefit remains thin, and several items are still allegations or self-reports.
Independent audit-level evidence on on-time, on-budget delivery and the causal split between AMLO policy and external tailwinds is still incomplete.
